title: Introduction & Licensing
examFocus: Medical requirements, CDL classes, endorsements, restrictions, disqualification rules — tested heavily on GK exam
summary: CDL classes, endorsements, restrictions, medical self-certification, and the disqualification rules examiners love to test.

topics.heading: The three CDL classes
bullets: Class A: any combination with a GCWR of 26,001+ lbs, as long as the towed unit's GVWR is over 10,000 lbs. Think tractor-trailers. Driving a Class A vehicle requires considerably more skill and knowledge than Classes B and C.

Class B: any single vehicle with a GVWR of 26,001+ lbs, or one towing something 10,000 lbs or less. Think straight trucks and large buses. Safely driving these requires more knowledge and skill than Class C vehicles.

Class C: doesn't meet A or B, but is either built for 16+ passengers (including the driver) or carries placarded hazardous materials. Some large Class C vehicles may require more skill than smaller ones, but licensing is based principally on the type of cargo carried.
Licenses stack downward: a Class A license also covers B and C vehicles; a Class B license also covers C.

topics.heading: Endorsements (extra letters on your CDL)
bullets: H – Hazardous materials. Requires a written test plus a TSA fingerprint background check. TSA and DOT require background checks on commercial drivers certified to transport hazardous materials.

N – Tank vehicle. Needed for tanks rated over 119 gallons individually and 1,000+ gallons combined, mounted permanently or temporarily. Liquids in bulk cause driving control problems because cargo is heavy, prone to shifting, and has a high center of gravity.

P – Passenger. Needed to drive any vehicle built to carry 16+ people including the driver. Must pass a special knowledge examination on safety considerations when transporting passengers and must pass skills tests in a passenger vehicle.
S – School bus. Must pass a special knowledge examination on safety considerations when transporting passengers in a school bus and must pass skills tests in a school bus.
T – Doubles/Triples. Considerable additional knowledge and skill is necessary to safely pull double and triple trailers in various traffic conditions.
X – Combination of tank + hazmat (hauling hazardous materials in a tank). Shows you have passed special knowledge examinations for both tank vehicles and hazardous materials.
Only P, S, and N can ever appear on a Commercial Learner's Permit (CLP). A CLP with P or S automatically carries a 'no passengers' restriction; a CLP with N carries a 'no cargo in tank' restriction.

topics.heading: Common restriction codes
bullets: E – no manual transmission (you tested in an automatic). For the skills test and restriction, an automatic transmission includes any transmission not operating fully on the gear shift and clutch principle.
K – intrastate only. If you certify as Non-Excepted Intrastate or Excepted Intrastate, you're restricted from operating a CMV in interstate commerce.

L – no air brakes. If you don't take or fail the air brake component of the knowledge test, or perform the skills test in a vehicle not equipped with air brakes. Air brakes include any braking system operating fully or partially on the air brake principle.
Z – no full air brakes (air-over-hydraulic only).
O – no fifth-wheel tractor-trailer combos (you tested with a pintle hook connection instead).
M – no Class A passenger vehicle (tested in a Class B passenger vehicle).
N – no Class A and B passenger vehicle (tested in a Class C passenger vehicle).
V – a medical variance is on file.

topics.heading: The testing path
bullets: Knowledge tests: general knowledge (everyone), plus air brakes, combination vehicles, passenger, school bus, tank, doubles/triples, or hazmat as needed for your endorsements.
Skills test has three parts, taken in this exact order, and you must pass each before moving on: vehicle inspection, basic vehicle control, then on-road driving.
You must test in the same class and configuration of vehicle you want licensed for.

topics.heading: Medical self-certification
bullets: You must declare interstate vs. intrastate commerce, and excepted vs. non-excepted status, when applying, renewing, upgrading, or transferring a CDL.
Most CDL holders driving in interstate commerce are 'non-excepted interstate' and must submit a current DOT medical examiner's certificate.
Failing to keep a required medical certificate current makes you 'not-certified' and you can lose your CDL.
As of December 11, 2025, medical examiner certificates are submitted electronically by the medical provider to FMCSA — Tax Collector's Offices no longer accept paper certificates.

topics.heading: Drug & Alcohol Clearinghouse (2024 update)
bullets: Beginning November 18, 2024, FLHSMV must obtain your driving record from the Commercial Driver's License Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse when applying, renewing, transferring, or changing a CDL/CLP.
If the Clearinghouse shows you are prohibited from operating a CMV, FLHSMV cannot issue, renew, transfer, or change your CDL/CLP.
FLHSMV must downgrade your CDL/CLP within 60 days of receiving prohibition notification from the Clearinghouse.
You will be notified immediately if prohibited, and you have 20 days to request an informal hearing.

topics.heading: Entry-Level Driver Training (ELDT)
bullets: Since February 7, 2022, entry-level drivers must complete ELDT before taking certain CDL skills or knowledge tests.
ELDT required for: first-time Class A or Class B CDL applicants, upgrading Class B to Class A, and first-time school bus (S), passenger (P), or hazardous materials (H) endorsements.
Training must be from an FMCSA-registered training provider.

topics.heading: Language requirements (2026 update)
bullets: As of February 6, 2026, all driver license knowledge and skills examinations are administered exclusively in English.
This change applies to all driver license classifications, including exams administered orally.
Interpreters may not be used during the administration of any CDL tests.

topics.heading: Residency requirements (2024 update)
bullets: Effective October 7, 2024, all CLP/CDL applicants or those updating an address must provide proof of Florida residency.
You must be a Florida resident to obtain a Florida CDL.

topics.heading: Disqualification numbers worth memorizing
bullets: BAC of 0.04% or higher, refusing an alcohol test, or driving a CMV under the influence of alcohol/drugs: lose your CDL for at least 1 year on a first offense (3 years if hauling placarded hazmat).
A second major offense (DUI, felony with a CMV, leaving the scene, causing a fatality through negligent operation) = disqualified for life.
Out-of-service order violation: 90 days minimum for a first offense, 1 year for a second within 10 years, 3 years for a third+.
Railroad-crossing violation: 60 days for a first offense, 120 days for a second within 3 years, 1 year for a third within 3 years.
Two serious traffic violations in a CMV within 3 years: at least 60 days disqualified. Three or more: at least 120 days.
Serious violations include going 15+ mph over the limit, reckless driving, improper lane changes, following too closely, and driving without the right class/endorsement.

Two or more convictions for using a hand-held phone or texting while driving a CMV: 60 days disqualified for the second offense, 120 for a third+, with fines up to $2,750 for the driver and $11,000 for the carrier.
Using a false name, making a false statement, or concealing a material fact in a CDL application: up to 5 years in prison, $5,000 fine, and suspension of driving privilege for at least 1 year.

topics.heading: Other rules that show up on the test
bullets: You may hold only one driver's license, period.
Notify your employer within 30 days of any traffic conviction (except parking), no matter what vehicle you were driving.
Notify your employer within 2 business days if your license is suspended, revoked, canceled, or you're disqualified.
Give a new employer your driving-job history for the past 10 years.
In Florida: minimum age is 18 for intrastate driving, 21 for interstate or hazmat; you must already hold a Florida Class E license.
It is illegal to permit or authorize an unlicensed person to drive a motor vehicle — can result in 60-day jail sentence and $500 fine for the person who authorizes it.

quiz.q: A single straight truck needs a Class B CDL once its GVWR reaches what weight?
quiz.explain: 26,001 lbs or more GVWR on a single vehicle puts it in Class B.

quiz.q: A combination vehicle needs a Class A CDL when the GCWR is 26,001+ lbs and the towed unit's GVWR is over how many pounds?
quiz.explain: The towed unit must be rated over 10,000 lbs GVWR for the combo to require Class A.

quiz.q: Which endorsement lets you drive a bus built to carry 16 or more people, including the driver?
quiz.explain: P is the Passenger endorsement.

quiz.q: Which of these endorsements can legally appear on a Commercial Learner's Permit (CLP)?
quiz.explain: Only P, S, and N may ever be added to a CLP.

quiz.q: Restriction code 'E' on a CDL means:
quiz.explain: E = restricted from operating a vehicle with a manual transmission.

quiz.q: What is the correct order of the three CDL skills test segments?
options: On-road driving, vehicle inspection, basic control
Basic control, on-road driving, vehicle inspection
Vehicle inspection, basic control skills, on-road driving
Vehicle inspection, on-road driving, basic control
quiz.explain: You must pass each segment in that order before moving to the next.

quiz.q: What blood alcohol concentration (BAC) makes it illegal to operate a CMV?
quiz.explain: 0.04% or higher is the illegal threshold for CMV drivers, well below the 0.08% car-driver limit.

quiz.q: A first BAC/DUI disqualification while hauling placarded hazardous materials costs you your CDL for at least:
quiz.explain: The hazmat load raises the minimum penalty to 3 years.

quiz.q: How many serious traffic violations within 3 years trigger a minimum 60-day CDL disqualification?
quiz.explain: Two serious violations within 3 years = at least 60 days disqualified.

quiz.q: Which of the following is considered a 'serious traffic violation' for CDL holders?
options: Driving 5 mph over the speed limit
Driving 15 mph or more over the speed limit
quiz.explain: Going 15+ mph over the limit is a serious violation.

quiz.q: What is the minimum disqualification period for a first railroad-crossing violation?
quiz.explain: 60 days for first offense, 120 days for second within 3 years, 1 year for third within 3 years.

quiz.q: You must notify your employer of any traffic conviction (except parking) within how many days?
quiz.explain: Within 30 days of any traffic conviction.

quiz.q: You must notify your employer within 2 business days if your license is:
options: Suspended, revoked, canceled, or you're disqualified
quiz.explain: Within 2 business days for suspension, revocation, cancellation, or disqualification.

quiz.q: What is the minimum age for intrastate CDL driving in Florida?
quiz.explain: 18 for intrastate, 21 for interstate or hazmat.

quiz.q: What is the minimum age for interstate CDL driving in Florida?
quiz.explain: 21 for interstate or hazmat.

quiz.q: A tank vehicle endorsement (N) is required for tanks with an individual rated capacity of more than:
quiz.explain: More than 119 gallons individually and 1,000+ gallons combined.

quiz.q: What does restriction code 'L' indicate?
quiz.explain: L = no air brake equipped CMV.

quiz.q: Using a false name or making a false statement in a CDL application can result in:
options: Up to 5 years in prison, $5,000 fine, and license suspension for at least 1 year
quiz.explain: Up to 5 years in prison, $5,000 fine, and suspension of driving privilege for at least 1 year.

quiz.q: How many driver's licenses may you hold?
quiz.explain: You may hold only one driver's license, period.

quiz.q: What is the minimum disqualification for a first out-of-service order violation?
quiz.explain: 90 days minimum for first offense, 1 year for second within 10 years, 3 years for third+.

quiz.q: Which endorsement requires a TSA fingerprint background check?
quiz.explain: Hazardous materials requires TSA fingerprint background check.

quiz.q: A second major offense (DUI, felony with a CMV, leaving the scene) results in:
quiz.explain: A second major offense = disqualified for life.

quiz.q: Beginning November 18, 2024, FLHSMV must obtain your driving record from which system when applying for a CDL?
options: The Commercial Driver's License Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse
quiz.explain: FLHSMV must check the Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse for CDL applications, renewals, transfers, and changes.

quiz.q: If the Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse shows you are prohibited from operating a CMV, FLHSMV must downgrade your CDL within how many days?
quiz.explain: FLHSMV must downgrade your CDL/CLP within 60 days of receiving prohibition notification.

quiz.q: As of December 11, 2025, how are medical examiner certificates submitted?
options: Electronically by the medical provider to FMCSA
quiz.explain: Medical providers now submit certificates electronically to FMCSA; Tax Collector's Offices no longer accept paper certificates.

quiz.q: Since February 7, 2022, entry-level drivers must complete ELDT before taking CDL tests for:
options: First-time Class A/B, upgrades to Class A, and first-time S/P/H endorsements
quiz.explain: ELDT required for first-time Class A/B, Class B to Class A upgrades, and first-time S/P/H endorsements.

quiz.q: As of February 6, 2026, all driver license knowledge and skills examinations are administered in:
quiz.explain: All examinations are administered exclusively in English as of February 6, 2026.

quiz.q: Effective October 7, 2024, all CLP/CDL applicants must provide proof of:
quiz.explain: Proof of Florida residency is required for all CLP/CDL applicants and address updates.

quiz.q: If you receive a prohibition notification from the Drug and Alcohol Clearinghouse, how many days do you have to request an informal hearing?
quiz.explain: You have 20 days to request an informal hearing after receiving a prohibition notification.

quiz.q: ELDT training must be completed from:
quiz.explain: Training must be from an FMCSA-registered training provider to meet ELDT requirements.

title: Driving Safely
examFocus: The bulk of the General Knowledge test — inspection, control, space management, speed, hazards, night/weather, emergencies, ABS, skids, fires, alcohol
summary: The biggest section on the general knowledge test: inspection, control, space, speed, hazards, night/weather driving, emergencies, ABS, skids, fires, and alcohol.

topics.heading: Vehicle inspection basics
bullets: The seven-step method: approach & look underneath, check the engine compartment, start the engine & check the cab, kill the engine & check lights, walk around the vehicle, check signal lights, do the final brake checks.
Air pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes on older single systems; the governor cuts out around 120-140 psi.
Minimum tread depth: 4/32 inch on steering (front) tires, 2/32 inch on all other tires.
More than 10 degrees of steering wheel play (about 2 inches of movement at the rim) is a problem.
Required emergency gear: fire extinguisher, spare electrical fuses (unless you have circuit breakers), and 3 reflective triangles (or 6 fusees or 3 liquid-burning flares).
Hydraulic brake check: pump the pedal 3 times, then hold firm pressure for 5 seconds — the pedal should not move.
Cargo securement must be re-checked within the first 50 miles, then every 150 miles or 3 hours, whichever comes first.

topics.heading: Basic control & shifting
bullets: When backing, always try to back toward the driver's side so you can see; use a helper and agree on a stop signal beforehand.
Downshift before you start down a hill or enter a curve — never after your speed has already built up.
Most heavy vehicles with unsynchronized manual transmissions require double-clutching; synchronized transmissions don't.
Turn retarders OFF whenever the road is wet, icy, or snow-covered — they can make the drive wheels skid.

topics.heading: Seeing & communicating
bullets: Look 12-15 seconds ahead — about one block in the city, a quarter mile on the highway.
Check mirrors regularly, and always before, during, and after a lane change, turn, or merge.
Signal early, hold the signal through the maneuver, and cancel it right after.

If you must stop on the road, place warning triangles within 10 minutes: on a two-lane road, one within 10 feet of the vehicle and one each 100 feet ahead and behind; on a divided or one-way road, at 10, 100, and 200 feet toward oncoming traffic. If a hill or curve blocks your visibility, move the back triangle to keep at least 500 feet of advance warning.

topics.heading: Speed & stopping distance
bullets: Total stopping distance = perception distance + reaction distance + braking distance.
At 55 mph in ideal conditions, total stopping distance is roughly 419 feet — nearly a football field and a half.
Doubling your speed roughly quadruples your stopping distance and impact force; tripling your speed multiplies both by about 9.
Cut speed by about a third on a wet road, by half or more on packed snow, and down to a crawl on ice.
Hydroplaning can happen at speeds as low as 30 mph if there's enough standing water.

topics.heading: Managing space
bullets: Following distance rule: 1 second for every 10 feet of your vehicle's length at speeds under 40 mph, plus 1 extra second if you're over 40 mph.
A loaded vehicle sits lower than an empty one of the same type — clearing a bridge loaded doesn't guarantee you'll clear it empty.
On right turns, keep the rear of your vehicle close to the curb rather than swinging wide left first — swinging left invites someone to pass you on the right.

topics.heading: Distracted, drowsy & impaired driving
bullets: Hand-held phone use and texting are both banned while driving a CMV. A second conviction means 60 days disqualified; a third means 120 days, plus fines up to $2,750 for the driver and $11,000 for the carrier.
Getting 6 hours of sleep or less roughly triples your crash risk.
Plan breaks about every 100 miles or 2 hours on long trips — the only real cure for drowsiness is sleep, not caffeine or fresh air.

topics.heading: Night, fog & winter driving
bullets: Low beams show the road about 250 feet ahead; high beams about 350-500 feet. Never outdrive your headlights.
Dim your high beams within 500 feet of an oncoming vehicle or one you're following.
The best advice for fog is simply: don't drive in it. If you must, use low beams and fog lights, not high beams.
Winter tread minimums are the same as always — 4/32 inch front, 2/32 inch other — but more is safer.

topics.heading: Railroad crossings
bullets: The round, black-on-yellow sign is the advance warning sign — it means slow down and be ready to stop.
If there's no stop line, stop between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail at a cross-buck sign.
A typical tractor-trailer needs about 14 seconds to clear a single track, and 15+ seconds to clear a double track — never get trapped stopping on the tracks.
Never shift gears while crossing the tracks.

topics.heading: Mountain driving & brake fade
bullets: Select your safe speed and downshift to the right gear BEFORE starting down a grade, not after you're already rolling.
Use engine braking as your main speed control; apply the brakes firmly enough for a real slowdown, then release — repeated hard, continuous braking causes brake fade.
Escape ramps use soft material (and often an upgrade) to safely stop a runaway vehicle — use one if your brakes fail.

topics.heading: Emergency maneuvers, ABS & skids
bullets: Steering around an obstacle is often faster and safer than trying to stop in time.
Controlled braking: brake as hard as possible without locking the wheels. Stab braking: brake fully, release the instant wheels lock, then reapply.
If a tire blows out, hold the wheel firmly and stay off the brake until you've slowed down — braking hard can cause loss of control.
ABS does not necessarily shorten stopping distance — it helps you keep steering control. Brake the same way you always would; don't pump the brakes.
To recover from a drive-wheel skid: stop braking to let the wheels roll again, and counter-steer. Never use the trailer hand valve to try to straighten a skidding trailer.

topics.heading: Accidents, fires & alcohol
bullets: Three steps at any accident: protect the area, notify authorities, care for the injured.
Fire extinguisher classes: A = wood/paper/ordinary combustibles, B = flammable liquids, C = electrical, D = combustible metals. Never use water on an electrical or gasoline fire.
A standard drink is about 12 oz of beer, 5 oz of wine, or 1.5 oz of 80-proof liquor — they all contain roughly the same amount of alcohol.
The liver only processes about one drink per hour; only time sobers you up, not coffee or a cold shower.

topics.heading: Hazardous materials — what every driver should know
bullets: There are 9 hazard classes. A placarded vehicle needs 4 identical placards: front, rear, and both sides.
You need a hazmat endorsement to legally drive a vehicle that requires placards.
Identification numbers on shipping papers are preceded by the letters 'UN' or 'NA'.

tips.heading: Double-clutching, step by step
tips.body: Since you're testing in a manual, examiners expect clean, silent shifts — no clashing gears. The sequence is the same for every shift: clutch in → shift to neutral → clutch OUT (briefly, in neutral) → clutch in again → shift into the next gear → clutch out. The 'blip' in neutral is what lets the gears sync without grinding.

tips.heading: Match your RPM, not just your gear
tips.body: Upshifting: let engine RPM drop toward your target before engaging the next gear. Downshifting: give the engine a quick throttle blip while in neutral to bring RPM UP to match the lower gear's speed before engaging it. Rushing this step is the #1 cause of grinding on the road test.

tips.heading: Shift by sound and feel, not the speedometer
tips.body: Watching the speedometer to decide when to shift means you're not watching the road. Learn your truck's engine sound at each shift point — most drivers shift by ear within a week of practice.

tips.heading: Never coast in neutral
tips.body: Besides being an automatic 'unsafe coasting' fault on the road test, coasting means you have no engine braking and (on some trucks) no power for your air compressor or steering assist. Stay in gear.

quiz.q: During the vehicle inspection, minimum tread depth on steering axle tires is:
quiz.explain: 4/32 inch on the front (steering) tires; 2/32 inch is the minimum for all other tires.

quiz.q: How much steering wheel play is too much?
quiz.explain: More than 10 degrees (about 2 inches of movement at the rim of a 20-inch wheel) makes steering unsafe.

quiz.q: To check hydraulic brakes for leaks, you should:
options: Pump the pedal 3 times, then hold firm pressure for 5 seconds and watch for movement
Press the pedal once and release immediately
Rev the engine while pressing the pedal
Check only the brake fluid color
quiz.explain: If the pedal moves after 5 seconds of held pressure, there's a leak or other problem.

quiz.q: After starting a trip, you must re-inspect cargo securement within the first:
quiz.explain: Then re-check every 150 miles or 3 hours after that, whichever comes first.

quiz.q: When backing a vehicle, you should generally back toward:
options: The passenger side, because it's wider
The driver's side, so you can see better
quiz.explain: Backing toward the driver's side lets you watch the rear by looking out your own window.

quiz.q: You should downshift to a lower gear:
options: After your vehicle has already picked up speed going downhill
Before starting down a grade or entering a curve
Only when the brakes start to fail
Only on manual transmissions with retarders
quiz.explain: Downshift ahead of time — trying to shift down after speed builds can fail and cost you engine braking.

quiz.q: Retarders should be turned OFF when the road is:
quiz.explain: On slippery roads, retarders can cause the drive wheels to skid.

quiz.q: Most good drivers look how far ahead while driving?
quiz.explain: 12-15 seconds ahead — roughly a city block at low speed, a quarter mile at highway speed.

quiz.q: On a two-lane road (traffic both directions), where should you place your three warning triangles if you must stop?
options: All three directly behind the vehicle
Within 10 feet of the vehicle, and 100 feet ahead and 100 feet behind
quiz.explain: One near the vehicle, one 100 feet ahead, one 100 feet behind, to warn traffic from both directions.

quiz.q: Total stopping distance is the sum of:
options: Reaction distance and braking distance only
Perception distance, reaction distance, and braking distance
quiz.explain: All three stack together to make up total stopping distance.

quiz.q: At 55 mph in good conditions, roughly how far does it take a heavy vehicle to stop completely?
quiz.explain: About 419 feet — nearly a football field and a half.

quiz.q: If you double your speed from 20 to 40 mph, your braking distance becomes roughly:
quiz.explain: Doubling speed roughly quadruples both impact force and braking distance.

quiz.q: On a wet road, you should generally reduce your speed by about:
quiz.explain: Cut speed by about a third on wet pavement; more on snow, and to a crawl on ice.

quiz.q: Hydroplaning can start at speeds as low as:
quiz.explain: With enough standing water, hydroplaning can occur at just 30 mph.

quiz.q: The following-distance rule of thumb is 1 second per 10 feet of vehicle length under 40 mph, plus:
options: 1 extra second if you're driving over 40 mph
Double the count in rain only
quiz.explain: Add 1 second if your speed is over 40 mph.

quiz.q: How many convictions for texting while driving a CMV trigger your first disqualification period?
quiz.explain: The second conviction brings a 60-day disqualification; a third or more brings 120 days.

quiz.q: Getting 6 hours of sleep or less before driving roughly:
quiz.explain: Sleep-deprived driving (6 hours or less) roughly triples crash risk according to the manual.

quiz.q: With low-beam headlights, you can typically see about how far ahead?
quiz.explain: Low beams show about 250 feet; high beams show about 350-500 feet.

quiz.q: You should dim your high beams when within how many feet of an oncoming or followed vehicle?
quiz.explain: Dim within 500 feet to avoid blinding other drivers.

quiz.q: The best advice given for driving in fog is:
options: Use your high beams for maximum visibility
Speed up to get through it faster
Don't drive in it — pull off and wait if you can
quiz.explain: If you must drive, use low beams and fog lights, and slow down well before entering the fog.

quiz.q: At a railroad crossing with no painted stop line, how far from the nearest rail should you stop?
options: Right up against the cross-buck sign
quiz.explain: Stop no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail.

quiz.q: About how long does it take a typical tractor-trailer to clear a single railroad track?
quiz.explain: About 14 seconds for one track, 15+ seconds for a double track.

quiz.q: When descending a long grade, your main method of controlling speed should be:
options: The braking effect of the engine, in a low gear
quiz.explain: Use engine braking as the principal control; use the brakes only in short, firm applications.

quiz.q: If a tire blows out while driving, you should:
options: Brake hard immediately to stop as fast as possible
Hold the wheel firmly and stay off the brake until you've slowed down
Turn sharply toward the shoulder right away
quiz.explain: Braking hard right after a blowout can cause you to lose control; slow down gradually first.

quiz.q: Does ABS necessarily shorten your stopping distance?
options: No — it mainly helps you keep steering control during hard braking
ABS has no effect on braking at all
quiz.explain: ABS keeps wheels from locking so you can steer; it doesn't guarantee a shorter stop.

quiz.q: To recover from a rear-wheel (drive-wheel) skid, you should:
options: Apply the trailer hand brake to straighten the rig
quiz.explain: Release the brakes to let the wheels roll again, then counter-steer — never use the trailer hand valve to fix a skid.

quiz.q: Which fire extinguisher rule is correct?
options: Water works fine on electrical fires
Never use water on an electrical fire or a gasoline fire
Class D extinguishers are for wood and paper
Class A fires require carbon dioxide only
quiz.explain: Water can cause shock on electrical fires and spread gasoline fires.

quiz.q: A standard alcoholic drink (12 oz beer, 5 oz wine, or 1.5 oz of 80-proof liquor) all contain roughly:
options: Twice as much alcohol in wine as beer
No comparable amount — it depends on brand only
quiz.explain: All three are considered equivalent standard drinks.

quiz.q: A placarded hazardous materials vehicle must display placards on:
options: All four sides — front, rear, and both sides
quiz.explain: Four identical placards: front, rear, and both sides.

quiz.q: Bonus (manual transmission): the correct double-clutch sequence for shifting is:
options: Clutch in, shift, clutch out — done in one motion
Clutch in, shift to neutral, clutch out, clutch in again, shift to next gear, clutch out
Hold the clutch down through the whole shift
Never use the clutch after the vehicle is moving
quiz.explain: The brief release in neutral is what lets engine and gear speed sync without grinding.

quiz.q: Bonus (manual transmission): when downshifting with the double-clutch method, you should:
options: Let RPM drop as low as possible before engaging the lower gear
Blip the throttle in neutral to bring RPM UP to match the lower gear
Skip the clutch entirely on downshifts
quiz.explain: A lower gear spins faster at the same road speed, so you rev-match upward before engaging it.

quiz.q: Bonus (manual transmission): grinding gears on the skills test is most often caused by:
options: Rushing the neutral pause and skipping the RPM-match step
Using too much clutch pedal travel
Shifting in a straight line instead of on a curve
quiz.explain: Take the extra half-second in neutral to match engine speed to the next gear.

quiz.q: Bonus (manual transmission): the safest way to know when to shift is to:
options: Learn to shift by the engine's sound and feel, keeping your eyes on the road
Shift at a fixed time interval regardless of speed
quiz.explain: Experienced drivers shift by ear so their eyes stay on traffic, not the gauges.

quiz.q: Bonus (manual transmission): coasting in neutral is discouraged because:
options: It's scored as unsafe coasting and you lose engine braking and other systems that rely on the engine running under load
It makes the transmission shift faster
quiz.explain: Stay in gear — coasting removes your engine braking and can starve systems like air brakes or power steering on some trucks.

quiz.q: You're driving a 40-foot truck at 35 mph. What's the minimum following distance you should leave?
quiz.explain: 1 second per 10 feet under 40 mph = 4 seconds for a 40-foot rig. Over 40 mph, add 1 more second.

quiz.q: To measure your following distance, you should:
options: Count seconds between when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed landmark and when you do
Count one Mississippi per car length
quiz.explain: Wait until the vehicle ahead passes a shadow, marking, or landmark, then count 'one-thousand-and-one…' until you reach it.

quiz.q: You're driving a 30-foot vehicle at 55 mph. How many seconds of following distance should you allow?
quiz.explain: 30 ft = 3 seconds under 40 mph, plus 1 extra second because you're over 40 mph = 4 seconds.

quiz.q: If a vehicle is following you too closely, you should:
options: Slow down and increase your following distance ahead
quiz.explain: Opening up space ahead gives you room to stop gradually if the tailgater forces a sudden slowdown.

title: Transporting Cargo Safely
examFocus: Cargo securement, weight distribution, and inspection — covered on General Knowledge exam
summary: Weight limits, balance, tie-downs, and special cargo that needs extra care.

topics.heading: Your responsibilities as the driver
bullets: Inspect your cargo, recognize overloads or poor weight balance, confirm it's properly secured, and make sure it doesn't block your view or your access to emergency equipment.
Re-inspect cargo and tie-downs within the first 50 miles of a trip, and then every 150 miles or 3 hours after that, whichever comes first.

topics.heading: Weight definitions
bullets: GVWR (Gross Vehicle Weight Rating): manufacturer's max loaded weight for one vehicle.
GCWR (Gross Combination Weight Rating): manufacturer's max loaded weight for a power unit plus everything it's towing.
Axle weight: weight transmitted to the ground by one axle or set of axles.
A bridge formula sets lower maximum axle weights for axles that sit closer together, to protect bridges and roads.

topics.heading: Keep it low and balanced
bullets: A high center of gravity (cargo piled high, or heavy cargo on top) makes rollover far more likely, especially in curves.
Too much weight on the steering axle makes steering hard; too little makes it dangerously light and hard to control.
Too little weight on the drive axles causes poor traction and wheel spin, especially in bad weather.

topics.heading: Securing cargo
bullets: Blocking and bracing keep cargo from sliding forward, back, or side to side.
Rule of thumb: at least one tie-down for every 10 feet of cargo, with a minimum of two tie-downs no matter how small the load.
Header boards ('headache racks') protect the cab from cargo sliding forward in a crash or hard stop.
Cover cargo both to protect people from spills and to protect the cargo from weather.

topics.heading: Cargo that needs extra caution
bullets: Dry bulk tanks: high center of gravity — go slow and easy through curves and turns.
Hanging meat: very unstable with a high center of gravity — slow way down on ramps and curves.
Livestock: can shift their weight, especially leaning into curves — use false bulkheads with a partial load.
Oversized loads: require special permits, signage, and sometimes escorts.

quiz.q: How soon after starting a trip must you re-check cargo securement?
quiz.explain: Within the first 50 miles, then every 150 miles or 3 hours after that.

quiz.q: After that first check, how often should you re-check cargo on a long trip?
quiz.explain: Every 150 miles or 3 hours, whichever happens first.

quiz.q: GCWR stands for and refers to:
options: Gross Cargo Weight Rating — the max weight of freight alone
Gross Combination Weight Rating — max weight of the power unit plus everything towed
quiz.explain: It's the manufacturer's maximum rating for the whole combination.

quiz.q: A high center of gravity from cargo piled up high mainly increases the risk of:
quiz.explain: High, top-heavy loads are far more likely to roll over.

quiz.q: The general tie-down rule of thumb is:
options: One tie-down for the whole load, regardless of size
At least one tie-down per 10 feet of cargo, minimum two
Exactly four tie-downs on every load
Tie-downs are optional if the cargo is under 500 lbs
quiz.explain: At least one per 10 feet of cargo, and never fewer than two, even on tiny loads.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of a header board (headache rack)?
options: To protect the cab if cargo shifts forward in a crash or hard stop
quiz.explain: It blocks cargo from sliding into the cab.

quiz.q: Too little weight on the drive axles mainly causes:
quiz.explain: Underloaded drive axles struggle for traction, especially in rain or snow.

quiz.q: Why is dry bulk cargo (like a dry bulk tank) tricky to haul?
options: It has a high center of gravity and the load can shift
It requires no tie-downs at all
quiz.explain: Go slow and careful on curves and sharp turns.

quiz.q: When hauling livestock, why is a partial load more dangerous than a full one?
options: Animals can shift and lean into curves, moving the center of gravity
quiz.explain: Use false bulkheads to bunch animals together and reduce shifting.

quiz.q: What are the two basic reasons for covering cargo on an open bed?
options: To improve mileage and reduce noise
To protect people from spilled cargo and to protect the cargo from weather
To hide the cargo from view and reduce weight
It's required only for hazardous materials
quiz.explain: Spill protection and weather protection are the two core reasons.

quiz.q: A bridge formula sets lower maximum axle weights for axles that are:
quiz.explain: Axles closer together get a lower max weight to avoid overloading bridges and roads.

quiz.q: Overloading a truck primarily hurts:
quiz.explain: Overloaded trucks climb slowly, gain too much speed downhill, and take longer to stop.

title: Transporting Passengers Safely
skipReason: For bus drivers only — not needed for Class A tractor-trailer, dump truck, or bucket truck
summary: Bus-specific inspection points, loading rules, hazmat limits on a bus, and the prohibited practices list.

topics.heading: Getting the P endorsement
bullets: Requires a knowledge test covering Sections 2 and 4 of the manual, plus Section 5 (air brakes) if your bus has them, and the passenger skills tests.

topics.heading: Extra inspection points for buses
bullets: Check handholds, railings, floor covering, emergency exit handles, and any restroom emergency buzzer.
Never drive with an open emergency exit door or window, and the 'Emergency Exit' sign must be clearly visible.

topics.heading: Hazardous materials on a bus
bullets: Buses may carry small-arms ammunition (ORM-D labeled), emergency hospital supplies, and drugs.

Buses can never carry: poison gas, more than 100 lbs of solid Class 6 poisons, explosives in a space occupied by people (except small-arms ammo), or labeled radioactive materials in a space occupied by people.
The overall limit for permitted hazardous materials on a bus is 500 lbs total, no more than 100 lbs of any single class.

topics.heading: The standee line
bullets: On buses designed to allow standing, a 2-inch line marks how far forward riders may stand. No one may stand ahead of the rear of the driver's seat.

topics.heading: Railroad crossings & drawbridges
bullets: Stop your bus between 15 and 50 feet before a railroad crossing, listen and look both ways, and open the forward door if it helps you see or hear.
Stop at least 50 feet before an unguarded drawbridge and make sure the draw is fully closed before crossing.

topics.heading: Prohibited practices
bullets: Don't refuel with riders aboard unless absolutely necessary, and never refuel inside a closed building with riders on board.
Don't talk with riders or do anything distracting while driving.
Don't tow or push a disabled bus with riders aboard unless getting off would be more dangerous.

topics.heading: Brake-door interlock
bullets: On some transit buses, opening the rear door automatically applies the brake and holds the throttle at idle. This is a safety feature — never use it as a substitute for the parking brake.

quiz.q: The standee line on a bus marks:
options: How far forward standing riders may go
quiz.explain: No rider may stand forward of the rear of the driver's seat.

quiz.q: What is the total weight limit for hazardous materials permitted aboard a bus?
options: 500 lbs total, no more than 100 lbs of any one class
There is no limit if properly labeled
quiz.explain: 500 lbs total, capped at 100 lbs per class.

quiz.q: Which of these can a bus legally carry?
options: Labeled radioactive material in the passenger space
quiz.explain: ORM-D small-arms ammo, emergency hospital supplies, and drugs are allowed in small amounts.

quiz.q: How far before a railroad crossing must a bus stop?
quiz.explain: Stop between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail.

quiz.q: At an unguarded drawbridge with no signal or attendant, how far before the draw must you stop?
quiz.explain: Stop at least 50 feet before the draw and confirm it's fully closed.

quiz.q: Refueling a bus with riders aboard is:
options: Allowed only if absolutely necessary, and never inside a closed building
quiz.explain: Avoid it when possible; never do it inside a closed building with riders on board.

quiz.q: A brake-door interlock on a transit bus:
options: Replaces the need for a parking brake
Applies the brake and holds idle when the rear door opens, but is not a substitute for the parking brake
Only works when the bus is empty
quiz.explain: It's a safety feature, not a parking brake replacement.

quiz.q: Should you tow or push a disabled bus with riders aboard?
options: Only to the nearest safe spot to let riders off, and only if getting off would be unsafe
quiz.explain: Only move to the nearest safe unloading spot, and only if it's unsafe for riders to exit first.

quiz.q: What should you never drive with, on a bus?
options: An open emergency exit door or window
quiz.explain: All emergency exits must be closed while driving, and the exit sign must be visible.

quiz.q: Before crossing a drawbridge, you must:
options: Confirm the draw is fully closed
quiz.explain: Look to make sure the draw is completely closed before proceeding.

quiz.q: Which items must you check on a bus's interior before driving?
options: Handholds, railings, floor covering, and emergency exit handles
quiz.explain: All of these safety-related interior items must be checked.

quiz.q: To get a Passenger (P) endorsement, your knowledge test covers which manual sections (plus air brakes if applicable)?
quiz.explain: Sections 2 (Driving Safely) and 4 (Transporting Passengers), plus Section 5 if your bus has air brakes.

title: Air Brakes
examFocus: CRITICAL for bucket trucks and dump trucks — entire Air Brakes test (25 questions) is based on this section
summary: Every pressure number, timing, and warning threshold the air brake test is built around.

topics.heading: Three systems in one
bullets: Service brakes: the normal brakes you use with the pedal during driving.
Parking brakes: hold the vehicle when parked, using spring pressure held back by air pressure.
Emergency brakes: use parts of the service and parking brake systems to stop the vehicle if the air brake system fails.

topics.heading: The pressure numbers to memorize
bullets: Governor cuts out (stops the compressor) around 125 psi and cuts back in around 100 psi.
The safety relief valve is usually set to open at 150 psi — if it ever releases air, something's wrong.
Low air pressure warning must activate before air pressure drops below 55 psi (or one-half the governor cut-out pressure on older vehicles).
Spring brakes activate fully somewhere in the 20-45 psi range (typically 20-30 psi) — don't wait for them; stop safely the moment the low air warning comes on.
On large buses, low pressure warning devices often signal at 80-85 psi.
Dual air systems should build from 85 to 100 psi within 45 seconds with the engine running; older single air systems build 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes at idle.

topics.heading: Leak-rate limits (the exact numbers examiners ask about)
bullets: With the engine off and brakes released, air loss should be less than 2 psi/minute for a single vehicle, less than 3 psi/minute for a combination vehicle.
With the foot brake held down for 1 minute, loss should be no more than 3 psi/minute (single vehicle) or 4 psi/minute (combination vehicle).

topics.heading: Slack adjusters & brake types
bullets: If a slack adjuster moves more than about 1 inch when pulled by hand, it likely needs adjustment.
Vehicles built since 1994 have automatic slack adjusters, but you should still check them — don't rely on manual adjustment as a real fix.
S-cam drum brakes are the most common type — air pressure pushes the rod out, moving the slack adjuster and twisting the brake camshaft.
Wedge brakes: the brake chamber push rod pushes a wedge directly between the ends of two brake shoes.
Disc brakes: air pressure acts on a brake chamber and slack adjuster, but a 'power screw' clamps the disc between brake lining pads like a large c-clamp.
Wedge brakes and disc brakes are less common than s-cam brakes.

topics.heading: Brake fade & overheating
bullets: Brake fade happens from overheating; brakes out of adjustment fail first, overloading the rest and accelerating fade.
If the application pressure gauge shows you need to increase pressure to hold the same speed, your brakes are fading — slow down and use a lower gear.
Increased application pressure can also be caused by brakes out of adjustment, air leaks, or mechanical problems.

topics.heading: Stopping distance with air brakes
bullets: Air brakes add 'brake lag' — about half a second, or roughly 32 feet at 55 mph — on top of the usual perception + reaction + braking distance.

topics.heading: Using air brakes correctly
bullets: Never push the brake pedal down while the spring (parking) brakes are set — it can damage them from combined spring and air pressure forces.
Never use the parking brake if the brakes are extremely hot or extremely wet in freezing weather.
Drain air tanks daily unless you have automatic drains — water can freeze in cold weather and cause brake failure.
Compressed air contains water and compressor oil which collect at the bottom of tanks and must be drained.
Some systems have an alcohol evaporator to reduce ice risk in cold weather — check the alcohol container daily during cold weather.
Pressing and releasing the pedal unnecessarily lets air out faster than the compressor can replace it — if pressure gets too low, brakes won't work.

topics.heading: Front brake limiting valves (older vehicles)
bullets: Some vehicles built before 1975 have a front brake limiting valve with 'normal' and 'slippery' positions.
The 'slippery' position cuts normal air pressure to front brakes by half to reduce skid risk.
However, limiting valves actually reduce stopping power — front wheel braking is good under all conditions.
Tests show front wheel skids from braking are not likely even on ice — keep the control in 'normal' position.
Many newer vehicles have automatic front wheel limiting valves that reduce air to front brakes except during hard braking (55+ psi application).

topics.heading: ABS requirements
bullets: Truck tractors with air brakes built on or after March 1, 1997 must have ABS.
Other air brake vehicles (trucks, buses, trailers, converter dollies) built on or after March 1, 1998 must have ABS.
Vehicles with ABS have yellow malfunction lamps — tractors/trucks/buses on the instrument panel, trailers on the left side front or rear corner.
On newer vehicles, the ABS lamp comes on at start-up for bulb check then goes out quickly; on older systems it may stay on until driving over 5 mph.
If the ABS lamp stays on after bulb check or comes on while driving, you may have lost ABS control at one or more wheels.
ABS is an addition to normal brakes — it doesn't decrease or increase normal braking capability and only activates when wheels are about to lock up.

tips.heading: The number ladder — memorize it in order, low to high
tips.body: Spring brakes fully apply: ~20-45 psi  →  Low-air warning must trigger: below 55 psi  →  Governor cuts IN (starts building air again): ~100 psi  →  Governor cuts OUT: ~125 psi  →  Safety relief valve: ~150 psi. Say this ladder out loud a few times — it's the backbone of both the written test and the vehicle inspection test.

tips.heading: The '2-3-3-4' leak-rate trick
tips.body: Engine off, brakes released: 2 psi/min single, 3 psi/min combo. Foot brake held: 3 psi/min single, 4 psi/min combo. Notice combination vehicles always get the bigger number in both tests — more air lines, more allowed leakage.

tips.heading: Practice the 3-part air brake check out loud
tips.body: The examiner wants to hear you narrate: (1) hold the foot brake 1 minute and watch the gauge, (2) fan the brakes and watch for the warning light/buzzer before 55 psi, (3) keep fanning until the rig's parking brakes pop on by themselves. Rehearse the script, not just the actions.

quiz.q: Around what pressure does the governor typically cut out (stop the compressor)?
quiz.explain: Around 125 psi cut-out, with cut-in around 100 psi.

quiz.q: The safety relief valve is usually set to open at approximately:
quiz.explain: 150 psi — if it releases air, get it checked.

quiz.q: The low air pressure warning signal must activate before pressure drops below:
quiz.explain: It must warn you before pressure falls below 55 psi.

quiz.q: Spring brakes typically apply fully somewhere in what pressure range?
quiz.explain: Commonly 20-30 psi within the broader 20-45 psi range — don't wait for this to happen automatically.

quiz.q: A dual air system should build from 85 to 100 psi within how many seconds, with the engine running?
quiz.explain: 45 seconds is the benchmark for dual systems; older single systems get 3 minutes for a bigger 50-90 psi build.

quiz.q: With the engine off and brakes released, an acceptable air leak rate for a single vehicle is:
options: Leak rate doesn't matter if the warning light works
quiz.explain: Under 2 psi/min for a single vehicle; under 3 psi/min for a combination vehicle.

quiz.q: Holding the foot brake down for 1 minute, the maximum acceptable leak rate for a combination vehicle is:
quiz.explain: 4 psi/minute max for combination vehicles (3 psi/minute for a single vehicle).

quiz.q: If a slack adjuster moves more than about how far when pulled by hand, it likely needs adjustment?
quiz.explain: About 1 inch of movement at the push rod is the rule of thumb.

quiz.q: Air brakes add extra stopping distance compared to hydraulic brakes because of:
options: Brake lag — the time for air to travel through the lines
quiz.explain: Brake lag adds about half a second (32 feet at 55 mph) to stopping distance.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of the air compressor governor?
options: To drain water from the air tanks
To control when the compressor pumps air into the storage tanks
quiz.explain: The governor stops the compressor at cut-out (~125 psi) and restarts it at cut-in (~100 psi).

quiz.q: Why must air tanks be drained regularly?
options: To remove water and compressor oil that can freeze and cause brake failure
quiz.explain: Water and oil collect at the bottom of tanks and can freeze in cold weather, causing brake failure.

quiz.q: What is a supply pressure gauge used for?
options: To tell you how much pressure is in the air tanks
quiz.explain: Supply pressure gauges show air tank pressure; dual systems have one gauge for each half or a single gauge with two needles.

quiz.q: What does the application pressure gauge show?
options: How much air is in the tanks
How much air pressure you are applying to the brakes
quiz.explain: It shows brake application pressure. If you need to increase pressure to hold the same speed, brakes are fading.

quiz.q: What is the 'wig wag' device?
options: A mechanical arm that drops into your view when air pressure drops below 55 psi
quiz.explain: The wig wag is a low air pressure warning device — automatic types rise back out of view when pressure is above 55 psi.

quiz.q: What are spring brakes?
options: Brakes that use only air pressure
Brakes held on by powerful springs when air pressure is removed
Brakes that only work on the front wheels
quiz.explain: Spring brakes are held back by air pressure during driving; if air is lost, the springs apply the brakes.

quiz.q: When should you stop driving if the low air pressure warning comes on?
options: When the spring brakes come on automatically
Immediately when the warning light and buzzer first come on
When you reach a truck stop
quiz.explain: Stop right away when the warning first activates — don't wait for spring brakes to come on automatically.

quiz.q: What is the most common type of foundation brake?
quiz.explain: S-cam drum brakes are the most common type — air pressure pushes the rod, moving the slack adjuster and twisting the camshaft.

quiz.q: Truck tractors with air brakes built on or after what date must be equipped with ABS?
quiz.explain: March 1, 1997 for truck tractors; March 1, 1998 for other air brake vehicles.

quiz.q: If the ABS malfunction lamp stays on after the bulb check, what does it mean?
options: You may have lost ABS control at one or more wheels
quiz.explain: A steady ABS lamp indicates loss of ABS control at one or more wheels — have it checked.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of an alcohol evaporator in an air brake system?
options: To reduce the risk of ice in air brake valves during cold weather
quiz.explain: Alcohol evaporators put alcohol into the system to prevent ice formation in cold weather.

quiz.q: What is a dual air brake system?
options: Two separate air systems — if one fails, the other still operates
Brakes on both front and rear wheels
quiz.explain: Dual systems have two separate air halves — if one fails, the other can still operate the brakes.

quiz.q: What is the proper way to use parking brakes on a vehicle with a modulating control valve?
options: Move the lever as far as it will go and hold it in place with the locking device
quiz.explain: When parking with a modulating valve, move the lever fully and lock it in place.

quiz.q: You should never push the brake pedal down when:
quiz.explain: Doing so can combine spring force and air pressure and damage the brakes.

quiz.q: How often should you drain air tanks manually, if they lack automatic drains?
options: At the end of each day of driving
Only when the low-air light comes on
quiz.explain: Daily draining removes water and oil that can freeze or damage the system.

quiz.q: Vehicles built since what year are required to have automatic slack adjusters?
quiz.explain: 1994 and later — but you should still check them during inspection.

quiz.q: Using the parking brake is unsafe when:
options: The vehicle is on level ground
The brakes are extremely hot, or extremely wet in freezing weather
You're parked for less than 10 minutes
quiz.explain: Extreme heat can damage hot brakes; freezing temps can freeze wet brakes so the vehicle can't move.

quiz.q: On an older vehicle whose governor cuts out at 120 psi, the low-air warning signal must come on no later than:
options: One-half the governor cut-out pressure (60 psi)
quiz.explain: The manual allows one-half the compressor governor cut-out pressure on older vehicles instead of the standard 55 psi.

title: Combination Vehicles
examFocus: CRITICAL for pulling trailers — entire Combination Vehicles test (20 questions) is based on this section
summary: Rollover and crack-the-whip risk, trailer air brake parts, and the coupling/uncoupling sequence.

topics.heading: Rollover risk
bullets: More than half of truck driver deaths in crashes are the result of truck rollovers.
Fully loaded rigs are about 10 times more likely to roll over in a crash than empty ones.
Keep cargo low and centered, and slow way down before curves, ramps, and turns — most rollovers happen because of too much speed in a turn, not bad luck.
Keeping cargo low is even more important in combination vehicles than in straight trucks.
If the load is to one side so it makes a trailer lean, a rollover is more likely — make sure cargo is centered and spread out as much as possible.

topics.heading: Crack-the-whip (rearward amplification)
bullets: A quick lane change can whip the rear trailer sideways hard enough to roll it over — many accidents involve only the trailer overturning.
Rearward amplification of 2.0 means the rear trailer is twice as likely to turn over as the tractor.
Triples have a rearward amplification of 3.5 — the last trailer is about 3.5 times as likely to roll as a five-axle tractor.
Steer gently and smoothly when pulling trailers — sudden steering movements can tip the trailer over.
Follow far enough behind other vehicles: at least 1 second for each 10 feet of vehicle length, plus another second if going over 40 mph.

topics.heading: Empty vs. loaded braking
bullets: Large combination vehicles take longer to stop when they are empty than when they are fully loaded.
When lightly loaded, very stiff suspension springs and strong brakes give poor traction and make it very easy to lock up the wheels.
Your trailer can swing out and strike other vehicles when lightly loaded.
Your tractor can jackknife very quickly when lightly loaded.
Bobtail tractors (tractors without semitrailers) are very hard to stop smoothly — tests show they take longer to stop than a tractor-semitrailer loaded to maximum gross weight.

topics.heading: Off-tracking & backing
bullets: The rear wheels follow a tighter path than the front wheels in a turn (off-tracking) — steer wide enough that the rear doesn't run over curbs or pedestrians, but keep the rear close to the curb to block others from passing on the right.
When backing a trailer, turn the steering wheel the OPPOSITE direction from a normal vehicle — and once the trailer starts turning, reverse your input to follow it.

topics.heading: Trailer air brake components
bullets: Trailer hand valve (trolley valve / Johnson bar): use ONLY to test trailer brakes, never while actually driving or for parking.
Tractor protection valve: closes automatically if air pressure drops into the 20-45 psi range, protecting the tractor's own air supply.
Trailer air supply control: a red, 8-sided knob — push in to supply air, pull out to shut off air and apply the trailer's emergency brakes.

Two air lines run to the trailer: the service line (also called the control/signal line) and the emergency line (also called the supply line). Losing pressure in the emergency line sets the trailer's emergency brakes.
Glad hand colors: blue = service line, red = emergency (supply) line.

topics.heading: Railroad-highway crossings with trailers
bullets: Trailers with low underneath clearance can get stuck on raised railroad crossings.
Low slung units at risk: lowboy, car carrier, moving van, possum-belly livestock trailer.
Single-axle tractor pulling a long trailer with landing gear set for a tandem-axle tractor can also get stuck.
If you get stuck, you may not have enough clearance to cross — check crossing height before attempting.

topics.heading: Shut-off valves
bullets: Shut-off valves (cut-out cocks) at the back of trailers must be OPEN — except at the very back of the last trailer in a combination, which must be CLOSED.

topics.heading: Coupling checks that matter
bullets: After coupling, there should be NO visible gap between the upper and lower fifth wheel — a gap means something is wrong.
Pull gently forward with the trailer brakes locked to confirm the kingpin is actually locked in.
Raise the landing gear fully before driving — never drive with it only partway up.

topics.heading: ABS on trailers
bullets: Trailers and converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998 are required to have ABS, shown by a yellow malfunction lamp on the left side of the trailer.

tips.heading: Pick your gear BEFORE you start backing or turning tight
tips.body: Get the trailer aimed and moving in first gear (or the gear your specific rig idles well in) before you start heavy steering input. Trying to shift mid-maneuver during the skills test, while also cranking the wheel, is when most manual-transmission drivers grind a gear.

tips.heading: Idle-speed control, not throttle control, for tight maneuvers
tips.body: For backing, alley dock, and offset exercises, cover the brake and feather the clutch instead of using the gas pedal. Let the engine idle do the work — it gives you far more precise, creep-speed control than trying to modulate the accelerator.

tips.heading: Rehearse the coupling walk-through out loud
tips.body: Before you back under the trailer: low-air/low-gear check, confirm trailer height, back in slowly, stop, check the gap (should be none), pull gently against the locked trailer brakes to test the kingpin, then hook air/electric lines and raise the landing gear fully. Examiners want to hear this sequence, not just see it.

quiz.q: Fully loaded combination rigs are how many times more likely to roll over in a crash than empty ones?
quiz.explain: About 10 times more likely — keep cargo low and centered.

quiz.q: In a set of triples, the rearward amplification of about 3.5 means:
options: The last trailer is 3.5 times as likely to roll over as the tractor
Triples are 3.5 times slower to accelerate
quiz.explain: The crack-the-whip effect is strongest on the very last trailer.

quiz.q: Compared to a fully loaded rig, a lightly loaded or bobtail tractor is:
options: Actually harder to stop smoothly, with poorer traction
Not affected by traction at all
quiz.explain: Stiff, lightly loaded suspension gives poor traction and can lock wheels easily.

quiz.q: When backing a trailer, you should turn the steering wheel:
options: The same direction you want the trailer to go, just like a car
The opposite direction from normal, then reverse once the trailer starts turning
Not at all until fully stopped
Only in small increments regardless of direction
quiz.explain: Trailer steering is reversed from normal car backing.

quiz.q: The trailer hand valve (trolley valve) should be used:
options: As your main brake while driving downhill
Only to test the trailer brakes, never while actually driving
Whenever the trailer starts to skid, to straighten it
quiz.explain: Using it while driving or to correct a skid can cause the trailer to skid worse.

quiz.q: The tractor protection valve closes automatically when air pressure drops into what range?
quiz.explain: It closes at 20-45 psi to protect the tractor's air supply.

quiz.q: What color is the trailer air supply control knob?
quiz.explain: It's a red, 8-sided knob — push in to supply air, pull out to shut off air.

quiz.q: Which glad hand color indicates the service (control) line?
quiz.explain: Blue = service line, red = emergency (supply) line.

quiz.q: More than half of truck driver deaths in crashes are the result of:
quiz.explain: More than half of truck driver deaths are from rollovers.

quiz.q: What is the minimum following distance for combination vehicles?
options: At least 1 second for each 10 feet of vehicle length
quiz.explain: At least 1 second for each 10 feet of vehicle length, plus another second if going over 40 mph.

quiz.q: Which type of trailer is most likely to get stuck on railroad crossings?
options: Low slung units like lowboys and car carriers
quiz.explain: Low slung units (lowboy, car carrier, moving van, possum-belly livestock) have low underneath clearance.

quiz.q: Shut-off valves at the back of trailers must be:
options: Open except at the very back of the last trailer, which must be closed
quiz.explain: All shut-off valves must be OPEN except the one at the very back of the last trailer.

quiz.q: After coupling, there should be:
options: A small gap between upper and lower fifth wheel
No visible gap between upper and lower fifth wheel
No gap visible from outside the cab
quiz.explain: No visible gap means proper coupling — a gap indicates something is wrong.

quiz.q: What should you do after coupling to confirm the kingpin is locked?
options: Pull gently forward with the trailer brakes locked
Check only the glad hand connections
quiz.explain: Pull gently forward against locked trailer brakes to confirm the kingpin is actually locked in.

quiz.q: Rearward amplification of 2.0 means:
options: The rear trailer is twice as likely to turn over as the tractor
The vehicle is twice as long
The trailer carries twice the weight
quiz.explain: A rearward amplification of 2.0 means the rear trailer is twice as likely to roll over as the tractor.

title: Doubles and Triples
skipReason: For driving 2-3 trailers hooked together — not needed for standard Class A single trailer operations
summary: Trailer order, converter dolly basics, and the shut-off valve pattern for multiple trailers.

topics.heading: Loading order
bullets: For the safest handling, put the heavier semitrailer in the FIRST position (right behind the tractor) and the lighter trailer in the rear.
Doubles and triples need more following distance and bigger gaps to enter or cross traffic — they're longer and cannot stop or turn as quickly.

topics.heading: Converter dollies
bullets: A converter dolly is one or two axles with a fifth wheel, used to couple an additional semitrailer behind the first one.
Converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998 must have ABS, shown by a yellow lamp on the left side of the dolly.

topics.heading: Shut-off valve pattern (multiple trailers)
bullets: Open at the rear of every trailer EXCEPT the very last one in the combination, which must be closed.
When checking, you should hear air escaping at each open point when the system is charged — confirming air reaches every trailer.

topics.heading: Coupling/uncoupling extra care
bullets: Never unlock the pintle hook while the converter dolly is still positioned under the rear trailer — the tow bar can fly up and cause injury.
Check trailer height carefully before backing a dolly under a trailer; it should sit slightly below the trailer's fifth wheel level so the trailer lifts as it's pushed under.

quiz.q: For the safest handling with doubles, which trailer should generally go in the first position behind the tractor?
quiz.explain: The heavier trailer up front, lighter trailer behind it.

quiz.q: A converter dolly is best described as:
options: One or two axles with a fifth wheel used to couple an extra semitrailer
quiz.explain: It lets you attach a second (or third) trailer behind the first.

quiz.q: Converter dollies built on or after what date must have ABS?
quiz.explain: Same requirement date as trailers: March 1, 1998.

quiz.q: In a set of triples, which shut-off valve position should be CLOSED?
options: The rear of the first trailer
The rear of the middle trailer
The rear of the very last trailer
quiz.explain: Only the rear of the last trailer in the combination is closed; everywhere else stays open.

quiz.q: Why should you never unlock the pintle hook while the dolly is still under the rear trailer?
options: The tow bar can fly up and cause injury
It will trigger the alarm system
It has no real danger, just inconvenience
quiz.explain: Pull the dolly out first, then unlock it once clear.

quiz.q: Doubles and triples require more following distance mainly because:
options: They're longer and can't stop or turn as quickly
State law requires extra distance only for triples
quiz.explain: More length means more space is needed to react safely.

quiz.q: When checking that air flows to all trailers in a set of doubles, what should you hear at an open shut-off valve?
quiz.explain: Hearing air escape confirms the system is charged all the way to the back.

quiz.q: Before backing a converter dolly under a rear trailer, the trailer height should be:
options: Much higher than the dolly's fifth wheel
Slightly lower than the dolly's fifth wheel, so it lifts as the dolly goes under
quiz.explain: The trailer should be slightly lower so the dolly raises it slightly during coupling.

quiz.q: The crack-the-whip effect in a set of triples is strongest on:
quiz.explain: Rearward amplification is greatest on the last trailer — about 3.5 times the tractor's movement.

quiz.q: A safe speed on a curve for a single-trailer combination:
options: Is always safe for doubles and triples too
May be too fast for doubles or triples
quiz.explain: Doubles and triples need slower speeds through curves due to their added length and rollover risk.

title: Tank Vehicles
skipReason: For liquid tanker trucks — not needed for dry van, flatbed, dump truck, or bucket truck operations
summary: High center of gravity, liquid surge, baffles, and outage — the physics of hauling bulk liquid.

topics.heading: High center of gravity
bullets: Liquid tankers are especially easy to roll over — tests have shown they can tip even at the posted speed limit for a curve.
Take highway curves and on/off ramps well BELOW the posted speed.

topics.heading: Liquid surge
bullets: Liquid surge (the wave of liquid moving in a partially full tank) can push a stopped truck forward, even shoving it into an intersection on a slippery surface.
Baffled tanks have internal bulkheads with holes that reduce forward-and-back surge, but not side-to-side surge.
Unbaffled ('smooth bore') tanks — often used for food-grade liquids because sanitation rules forbid baffles — have the strongest surge of all. Be extra cautious starting and stopping.

topics.heading: Outage
bullets: Outage is the deliberate empty space left in a tank so the liquid has room to expand as it warms.
How much to load depends on three things: how much the liquid will expand, its weight, and legal weight limits.

topics.heading: Driving technique
bullets: Start, slow down, stop, turn, and change lanes smoothly — abrupt inputs plus surge is a bad combination.
Brake early, keep steady pressure, and increase your following distance.
Empty tank vehicles can actually take longer to stop than full ones.

quiz.q: Liquid tankers can roll over:
options: Only if going far over the speed limit
Even at the posted speed limit for a curve
quiz.explain: High center of gravity makes them prone to rollover even at legal curve speeds.

quiz.q: What is 'liquid surge'?
options: The forward-and-back or side-to-side movement of liquid in a partially full tank
A type of brake fade specific to tankers
quiz.explain: Surge can push the vehicle in the direction the wave moves, even into an intersection on ice.

quiz.q: Baffled tanks help control:
quiz.explain: Baffles have holes that slow forward/back surge; side-to-side surge can still occur.

quiz.q: Why do many food-grade liquid tankers use unbaffled ('smooth bore') tanks?
options: Sanitation rules make baffles too hard to clean
They're required by DOT for all tankers
quiz.explain: Baffles are difficult to fully sanitize, so food-grade tanks often skip them — and have the strongest surge as a result.

quiz.q: Outage refers to:
options: Deliberately leaving room in the tank for liquid to expand
The maximum legal weight of a tanker
quiz.explain: Never load a tank totally full — liquids expand as they warm.

quiz.q: How much liquid you can load into a tank depends on:
options: Expansion amount, liquid weight, and legal weight limits
Only the color of the placard
quiz.explain: All three factors combine to set the safe/legal fill amount.

quiz.q: Compared to full tankers, empty tank vehicles:
options: Can actually take longer to stop
Are exempt from stopping distance rules
quiz.explain: Empty tankers can take longer to stop, similar to other empty heavy vehicles.

quiz.q: The recommended way to take curves and ramps in a tank vehicle is to:
options: Go slightly above the posted speed for momentum
Go well below the posted speed
Speed depends only on tank color
quiz.explain: Posted speeds may be too fast for a top-heavy, surging load.

quiz.q: Which driving habit is most important with a partially loaded tanker?
options: Braking and turning smoothly, and starting/stopping gradually
Accelerating hard to reduce trip time
quiz.explain: Smooth inputs reduce the danger from liquid surge.

title: Hazardous Materials
skipReason: For explosive/chemical trucks requiring placards — not needed unless you get the H endorsement later
summary: Hazard classes, shipping papers, placarding tables, and the driving/parking rules for hauling hazmat.

topics.heading: Why the rules exist
bullets: Contain the material (packaging rules for shippers, loading/unloading rules for drivers).
Communicate the risk (shipping papers, labels, placards).
Ensure safe drivers and equipment (endorsement, training, background checks).

topics.heading: The 9 hazard classes
bullets: 1 — Explosives (dynamite, fireworks)
2 — Gases (propane, oxygen, helium)
3 — Flammable liquids (gasoline)
4 — Flammable solids (matches)
5 — Oxidizers (ammonium nitrate, hydrogen peroxide)
6 — Poisons/toxic materials (pesticides, arsenic)
7 — Radioactive materials (uranium, plutonium)
8 — Corrosives (battery fluid, hydrochloric acid)
9 — Miscellaneous hazardous materials (asbestos, formaldehyde)
Plus ORM-D (other regulated material, like hairspray) and combustible liquids, which aren't numbered classes.

topics.heading: Shipping papers
bullets: Hazardous entries must be identified: entered first, highlighted, or marked with an X (or RQ for a reportable quantity) in the hazmat column.
Identification numbers are 4 digits, preceded by 'UN' or 'NA'.
Keep shipping papers within reach with your seat belt fastened, in a driver's-door pouch, or on the driver's seat when you're out of the vehicle.

topics.heading: Placarding basics
bullets: Placards must be at least 9.84 inches (250mm) square, diamond-shaped, and appear on all 4 sides: front, rear, both sides — 4 identical placards minimum.
Table 1 materials need placards for ANY amount you're carrying.
Table 2 materials only need placards once you're carrying 1,001 lbs or more total (across all shipping papers for that hazard class).

A 'DANGEROUS' placard can substitute for individual Table 2 placards when you have 1,001+ lbs total from two or more Table 2 classes, but no single class reaches 2,205 lbs (in which case you must use that class's specific placard).

topics.heading: Loading rules
bullets: Never smoke, or let anyone smoke, around Classes 1, 2.1, 3, 4, or 5 while loading or unloading.
Secure every hazardous materials package against movement.
Never transfer hazardous materials between packages while in transit (you may empty a cargo tank, but not other packages).

topics.heading: Driving & parking rules
bullets: A placarded vehicle must stop between 15 and 50 feet before a railroad crossing — same as passenger buses.
Never park a placarded vehicle within 300 feet of an open fire.
A person attending a parked placarded vehicle must be in the vehicle (awake, not in the sleeper) or within 100 feet with the vehicle in clear view.
Placarded power units must carry a fire extinguisher rated at least 10 B:C.
A 'safe haven' is an approved location where you may leave an explosives-laden vehicle unattended.
Never use burning flares or fuses near a flammable-liquid/gas tank or an explosives-laden vehicle — use reflective triangles or electric lights instead.

topics.heading: In an emergency
bullets: The Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG) is indexed by shipping name and identification number — first responders rely on it, so accurate paperwork saves lives.
At a hazmat scene: keep people away and upwind, warn others, call for help, and hand over your shipping papers to responders.

quiz.q: How many major hazard classes are there under the hazardous materials regulations?
quiz.explain: Nine numbered classes, plus ORM-D and combustible liquids as additional categories.

quiz.q: Hazardous materials identification numbers are preceded by which letters?
quiz.explain: A 4-digit ID number preceded by 'UN' or 'NA'.

quiz.q: Where may you legally keep hazmat shipping papers while driving?
options: In a pouch on the driver's door, or within reach with your seatbelt fastened
quiz.explain: Door pouch, within reach while belted, or on the driver's seat when you're out of the vehicle.

quiz.q: The minimum size for a placard is:
quiz.explain: At least 9.84 inches (250mm) square, diamond-shaped.

quiz.q: How many identical placards must a placarded vehicle display at minimum?
quiz.explain: Four: front, rear, and both sides.

quiz.q: Table 1 hazardous materials require placards:
options: Only when the vehicle is a tanker
quiz.explain: Table 1 materials must be placarded regardless of quantity.

quiz.q: Table 2 hazardous materials require placards once the total reaches:
quiz.explain: 1,001 lbs or more, combined across all shipping papers for that class.

quiz.q: You must never smoke while loading or unloading which hazard classes?
quiz.explain: Explosives, flammable gas, flammable liquids, flammable solids, and oxidizers — no smoking nearby.

quiz.q: How far before a railroad crossing must a placarded vehicle stop?
quiz.explain: Same rule as buses: stop between 15 and 50 feet from the nearest rail.

quiz.q: A placarded (non-explosive) vehicle may never be parked within how many feet of an open fire?
quiz.explain: 300 feet minimum distance from an open fire.

quiz.q: A person attending a parked placarded vehicle must be:
options: In the vehicle awake (not in the sleeper) or within 100 feet with a clear view
At least a quarter mile away
quiz.explain: Must be awake, aware of the hazard, and able to move the vehicle if needed.

quiz.q: What's the minimum fire extinguisher rating required on a placarded power unit?
quiz.explain: 10 B:C or higher.

quiz.q: Around a stopped vehicle carrying flammable liquids or gas, you should use as warning devices:
options: Reflective triangles or electric lights, never open flame
quiz.explain: Never use burning signals near flammable tanks or explosives.

quiz.q: What is a 'safe haven' in hazmat terms?
options: A rest stop with free coffee
An approved location to leave an explosives-laden vehicle unattended
A place you may never park hazmat loads
quiz.explain: Safe havens are designated by local authorities for parking explosives loads.

quiz.q: The Emergency Response Guidebook (ERG) is indexed by:
options: Proper shipping name and identification number
quiz.explain: First responders look up the shipping name or ID number to find handling guidance.

quiz.q: Which hazard class covers gasoline?
quiz.explain: Gasoline is the classic example of a Class 3 flammable liquid.

title: School Buses
skipReason: For school bus drivers only — not needed for Class A commercial trucking
summary: Danger zones, mirror systems, loading/unloading timing, railroad crossings, and evacuation rules.

topics.heading: The danger zone
bullets: Extends up to 30 feet from the front bumper (the first 10 feet is the most dangerous), 10 feet from each side, and 10 feet behind the rear bumper.
The left side of the bus is always considered dangerous because of passing traffic.

topics.heading: Four mirror systems
bullets: Flat mirrors (left/right front corners): should show about 200 feet (4 bus lengths) behind the bus, the sides, and the rear tires touching the ground.
Convex mirrors (below the flats): wide-angle view of the sides, but distort size and distance.
Crossover mirrors (front corners): show the danger zone directly in front of and beside the bus that you can't see directly.
Overhead inside mirror: monitors student activity inside the bus.

topics.heading: Loading timing
bullets: Activate alternating flashing amber lights about 200 feet (roughly 5-10 seconds) before the stop.
Turn on the right turn signal about 100-300 feet (roughly 3-5 seconds) before pulling over.
Stop with the front bumper at least 10 feet from the students — this forces them to walk into your view.
Put the transmission in park (or neutral) and set the parking brake at every stop.

topics.heading: Unloading & road-crossing
bullets: Have students exit and walk at least 10 feet away from the side of the bus to a point where you can plainly see them.
Students crossing in front of the bus should stop at the front-right corner, check for your signal, and cross only when you signal it's safe.
Never back a school bus with students outside of it.

topics.heading: Railroad crossings
bullets: Stop no closer than 15 feet and no farther than 50 feet from the nearest rail.
Turn off radios and silence passengers, open the service door and driver's window, and look/listen for a train.
Cross in a low gear and never change gears while crossing.
